I design machines, then write the software that makes them useful.

I design mechanisms in SolidWorks, wire and program the electronics, and write the software around them: ROS 2 and C++ on robots, Python and TypeScript for everything else. At Johns Hopkins I TA the robotics course RDKDC, build its ROS 2 setup, and write LLM tools for the Poverty & Inequality Research Lab.

INPUT

Soft leg: silicone bellows with printed form rings, about 2 bar.

BUILD

Extrusion frame, linear guide, digital spring balance.

why?

The leg rides on a ball-bearing slider, so its push goes straight into the spring balance and the reading is thrust only.

TEST

Arduino and AccelStepper swept the RPM underwater.

OUTPUT

0.6–0.7 kg peak at about 46 RPM, then a sharp drop.

why?

Past about 46 RPM the IP65 stepper hit its torque limit against the water's resistance.

    About

    I naturally look for ways to eliminate repetitive and tedious work through automation, so I can spend more time on the problems I enjoy most: designing, building, testing, debugging, and finding creative solutions when there is no obvious answer.

    I taught myself programming, which is partly why I chose Mechanical Engineering for my bachelor’s. I figured software was something I could keep learning on my own while gaining the hands on understanding of how real machines are designed and built. So now I know how to build some machines and put some code in them until they somehow work. I’m still working my way through electronics, but fortunately I have friends.

    Wait... mechanical + software + electronics. That’s robotics, isn’t it?

    I’m currently pursuing M.S.E Robotics at Johns Hopkins University, with experience across ROS2, autonomous mobile robots, robotic sorters, mechanical design, backend systems, automation tools, and real-world robotics deployment.

    Currently looking for full-time opportunities in robotics, automation, AI/ML, or software engineering in the United States.
